Absolution

/ab-suh-LOO-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Absolution means the formal act of being forgiven or released from guilt, wrongdoing, or sin.

Years after his harsh treatment of the team, the retired coach wrote to a former player asking for absolution.

Worked Example

At the reunion dinner, the aging partner quietly asked his old colleague for absolution for the promise he had broken when they dissolved the firm.

He is asking to be formally released from the guilt of a real, old wrong — not claiming he was right, just seeking to have the guilt lifted — which is precisely what absolution means.

How Absolution Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

forgiveness

forgiveness: the pardoning of a wrong someone committed

pardon

pardon: official forgiveness for an offense

remission

remission: formal release from guilt or a penalty

Antonyms

blame

blame: responsibility assigned for a fault or wrong

censure

censure: formal, public disapproval

How Strong Is It? — excuse → absolution → redemption

excuse vs. absolution

excuse vs. absolution: An excuse lets a small fault pass with a shrug; absolution formally wipes away the guilt of a real wrong.

redemption vs. absolution

redemption vs. absolution: Absolution releases a person from guilt for a wrong; redemption goes even further, restoring them completely, as if the wrong had been washed away.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ab-

Prefix — ab-: away, from

Root — solut

Root — solut: loosened, released (Latin solvere, 'to loosen')

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: noun-forming suffix: act or state of

Put it together

Put it together: Absolution is literally 'the act of loosening away' — guilt is untied from a person and released, leaving them free of it.

Use the root in a new word: absolve

Use the root in a new word: absolve: The review board voted to absolve the ranger of any responsibility for the fire, releasing her from all blame.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal / moral & religious

Absolution often carries a religious or moral flavor — a priest grants absolution, or a wronged person grants it for an old hurt. Keep it distinct from two words taught in other lessons: vindication (being cleared of blame or proven right — the person did nothing wrong) and clemency (mercy shown to someone who is guilty, like a reduced sentence). Absolution sits between them: the wrong was real, and it is formally forgiven.
